read.sections.0.heading.source: Your feed is chosen for you
read.sections.0.heading.back: Your feed is chosen for you

read.sections.0.text.source: People post far more than anyone could see, so many apps use an algorithm to choose what goes in your feed. An algorithm is a set of steps a computer follows. It learns from what you watched, liked or skipped before. Then it guesses what you will want to see. Apps aim for different things. Some count how long you watch, and some also ask people if they were happy with what they saw. A feed can be very useful. It can help you discover a skill, a song or local news you would never have found. In the made-up town of Maplebrook, Lena liked posts about books, and her feed found her a free video lesson on writing stories. Ravi watched many football videos, so his feed showed him mostly posts about the new sports field.
read.sections.0.text.back: People post far more than anyone could see, so many apps use an algorithm to choose what goes into your feed. An algorithm is a set of steps a computer follows. It learns from what you have watched, liked or skipped. Then it guesses what you will want to see. Each app has different aims. Some count how long you watch, and some also ask people whether they were satisfied with what they saw. A feed can be very useful. It can help you discover a skill, a song or local news that you could never have found yourself. In Maplebrook, a made-up town, Lena liked posts about books, and her feed led her to a free video lesson on writing stories. Ravi watched many football videos, so his feed mostly showed posts about the new sports field.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Feeds and what a town knows
read.sections.1.heading.back: Feeds and what a town knows

read.sections.1.text.source: Each feed is chosen for one person. So two neighbours can see very different posts about the same town, as Ravi and Lena did before Maplebrook's vote. This matters for public life. To take part in an election, people need some shared, correct facts, such as the day of the vote. A rumour can spread fast. In 2018, researchers at MIT in the United States published a study of about 126,000 news stories shared on Twitter from 2006 to 2017. False stories spread further and faster than true ones. People did most of the sharing, not robot accounts. The study looked at what people shared on one site, so it did not show that feeds or AI caused the spread.
read.sections.1.text.back: Each feed is chosen for one person. So two neighbours can see very different posts about the same town, like Ravi and Lena before the vote in Maplebrook. This matters for public life. To take part in an election, people need some correct facts that are shared by everyone, such as the day of the vote. A rumour can spread quickly. In 2018, researchers at MIT in the United States published a study of about 126,000 news stories shared on Twitter from 2006 to 2017. False stories spread further and faster than true stories. Most of the sharing was done by humans, not robot accounts. The study looked at what people shared on one site, so it does not show that feeds or AI caused that spread.

The stories were from 2006 to 2017. False stories spread faster than true ones. People shared them, not only robots. The study looked at what people shared on one site. read.sections.2.heading.source: What the evidence says, and what helps
read.sections.2.heading.back: What the evidence says, and what helps

read.sections.2.text.source: Some people worry that feeds put each of us in a filter bubble, where we only see one side. But in 2022, a review of many studies by the Reuters Institute at the University of Oxford found that real filter bubbles are less common than many people think. People's own choices about what to follow also matter. A European Union law, in full use since 2024, says that very large apps must explain how their feeds choose posts. They must also offer a feed that isn't based on what they know about you. Apps change often, so a study from a few years ago may not describe them today. You can help as well: follow different sources, share the official notice and check before you share.

watch.summary.source: This short news video for young people explains social media algorithms. An algorithm is a set of instructions that tells a computer program what to do. On many apps, the algorithm decides which posts you see and in what order. It also decides which posts you don't see. So when you scroll, you might think you are seeing everything. In fact, someone built a system that chooses for you. How does it choose? It tries to show you posts that will keep you interested, so you keep scrolling. Experts in the video say this isn't always a good thing. Your feed is carefully chosen. It is not a full view of the world. Knowing how your feed is chosen can help you think about what you see.
watch.summary.back: This short news video for young people explains social media algorithms. An algorithm is a set of instructions that tells a computer program what to do. In many apps, the algorithm decides which posts you see and in what order. It also decides which posts you do not see. So when you scroll, you might think you are seeing everything. In fact, someone has built a system that chooses for you. How does it choose? It tries to show posts that will keep you interested, so that you keep scrolling. Experts in this video say this is not always good. Your feed is carefully chosen. It is not a full picture of the world. Knowing how your feed is chosen can help you think about what you see.

educatorNotes.0.source: The research in section 2 is Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (Science, March 2018; MIT News, 8 March 2018, re-read 8 November 2026): about 126,000 cascades of news stories on Twitter, 2006 to 2017, tweeted over 4.5 million times by about 3 million people, each story judged true or false by six independent fact-checking organisations that agreed over 95% of the time. False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted, and true stories took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people; the gap held with bots removed. Its scope: one platform, those years, and stories that fact-checkers had investigated (contested stories, not all posts). It measured what people retweeted, not how a ranking algorithm chose posts, so it does not show that AI caused the spread; the authors say other platforms need separate study, and that they “cannot claim that novelty causes retweets”.
educatorNotes.0.back: The research in part 2 is Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (Science, March 2018; MIT News, 8 March 2018, re-read 8 November 2026): about 126,000 sharing cascades of news on Twitter, 2006 to 2017, tweeted more than 4.5 million times by about 3 million people, each story judged true or false by six independent fact-checking organisations that agreed more than 95% of the time. False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted, and true news took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people; the gap remained even with bots removed. Its scope: one platform, those years, and stories investigated by fact-checkers (disputed stories, not all posts). The study measured what people retweeted, not how a ranking algorithm chose posts, so it does not show that AI caused the spread; the authors say other platforms need to be studied separately, and that they “cannot claim that novelty causes retweets”.
educatorNotes.0.note: The quotation is translated into Malay; the original English is in the source note.

educatorNotes.1.source: Apps rank posts with different signals and aims; don't reduce them to one motive. For example, YouTube's help page lists watch and search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “not interested” and satisfaction surveys (to understand satisfaction, “not just watch time”). Filter bubbles: the Reuters Institute's 2022 review (Ross Arguedas, Robertson, Fletcher and Nielsen) found echo chambers “much less widespread than is commonly assumed”, “no support for the filter bubble hypothesis”, and an important role for people's own choices (self-selection); research outside the United States is limited. The European rule is the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065): in force 16 November 2022, applying in full from 17 February 2024, and earlier to very large platforms (over 45 million monthly users in the EU), four months after the Commission designated them; they must explain the main settings of their recommender systems, offer one not based on profiling, and assess risks such as the manipulation of elections.
educatorNotes.1.back: Apps rank posts with different signals and aims; don't reduce them to only one motive. For example, YouTube's help page lists watch and search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “not interested” and satisfaction surveys (to understand satisfaction, “not just watch time”). Filter bubbles: the Reuters Institute's 2022 review (Ross Arguedas, Robertson, Fletcher and Nielsen) found echo chambers “much less widespread than is commonly assumed”, “no support for the filter bubble hypothesis”, and an important role for people's own choices (self-selection); research outside the United States is limited. The European rule is the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065): in force 16 November 2022, applying fully from 17 February 2024, and earlier for very large platforms (more than 45 million users a month in the EU), four months after the Commission designated their status; those platforms must explain the main settings of their recommender systems, offer one system not based on profiling, and assess risks such as the manipulation of elections.

educatorNotes.2.source: Section 3's point that apps change matters: the study's years (2006 to 2017) predate today's feeds, and Twitter is now called X. For discussion or on paper, put Ravi's and Lena's feeds side by side and ask what each friend sees, what each might miss, and how the election office's notice could reach both. There is no sorting task.
